## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{17}{17}{17}{17}{16}{16}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why can a model that generates a fluent, correct action still fail to complete an autonomous task?_

The difference between answering a prompt and completing a delegated task marks the boundary of agentic machine learning systems. A foundation model can propose the exact line of code needed to fix a race condition, yet the repository remains broken until software inspects the source tree, applies the patch, runs regression tests, and verifies the outcome. Delegating autonomous work therefore requires building an engineered machine around the model, not merely selecting capable weights. That machine resembles a complete computer: it possesses components that compute, remember, act on the external world, supervise execution, recover from faults, and learn from experience.

However, its central processing element differs fundamentally from any classical processor: it is an autoregressive model whose outputs are stochastic proposals rather than deterministic execution. A fluent proposal can be subtly wrong, and the model cannot vouch for its own correctness. The surrounding system exists to contain that reality. The runtime determines what data the model perceives, bounds the actions it may execute, persists critical state across interruptions, and verifies whether the task actually succeeded. Every decision consumes computational time and monetary budget that only accepted outcomes justify. Building an agentic system is thus an exercise in systems engineering: sizing the runtime machinery to the horizon, state, and authority that the task demands.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Trace the architectural evolution from predictive and generative machine learning to autonomous agentic systems
- Explain why a model's stochastic proposals require an external runtime to close the interaction loop
- Classify a delegated task by horizon, state, and authority to identify its systems engineering obligations
- Distinguish mechanically enforced sandbox bounds from external evidence that justifies task acceptance
- Calculate unchecked task reliability and cost per accepted task across multi-turn execution horizons
- Specify a five-part task contract that separates goal, environment, permitted actions, observations, and completion criteria

:::
## The Evolution of Machine Learning Systems {#sec-vol3-intro-evolution}

Agentic machine learning represents the third major architectural era in machine learning systems, building directly on the foundations of predictive pipelines and conversational foundation models. Tracing this progression clarifies why the systems abstractions, runtime guarantees, and operational metrics developed for earlier eras prove insufficient for autonomous workloads.

### Three eras of machine learning systems

Machine learning systems have evolved across three distinct operational paradigms:

1. **Predictive Machine Learning Systems**: Classical machine learning deploys models as stateless function approximators that map fixed inputs to structured outputs ($y = f(x)$). Canonical workloads include image classification, recommendation ranking, fraud scoring, and tabular regression. In these systems, the inference pipeline is deterministic, the input schema is rigid, and the execution boundary remains closed and static. Systems engineering focused primarily on model serving throughput, single-device memory layout, kernel fusion, and batch inference latency. Downstream application code consumed model scores directly, requiring neither conversational memory nor subsequent feedback loops.
2. **Generative Foundation Models**: The rise of large-scale autoregressive transformers shifted the discipline toward general-purpose representation and reasoning. Trained across internet-scale corpora on compute fleets of tens of thousands of accelerators, foundation models generate open-ended text, synthetic code, and multimodal tokens. Yet in standard conversational deployment, the interaction pattern remains **open-loop** and **human-mediated**. When a developer works with a conversational assistant, the human acts as the runtime controller: the user issues a prompt, inspects the generated response, manually copies code into an editor, executes commands in a terminal, interprets compiler errors, and pastes stack traces back into the prompt window. While the foundation model generates candidate tokens, the human provides the execution environment, maintains working memory across turns, diagnoses runtime failures, and verifies correctness.
3. **Agentic Machine Learning Systems**: Agentic systems replace the human in the inner control loop with an autonomous software runtime. Instead of requesting advice or static text, a user delegates an end-to-end objective: clone a software repository, reproduce a reported defect, synthesize a candidate fix, run the full test suite in an isolated sandbox, iterate until regressions clear, and return a verified patch. The foundation model shifts from an advisory conversational partner to an action-proposing component embedded within an active feedback loop.

```
Era 1: Predictive Systems (Stateless)
   Input [x] ───────► [ Model f(x) ] ───────► Output [y]

Era 2: Generative / Conversational AI (Human Closes the Loop)
   User Prompt ─────► [ Foundation Model ] ──► Candidate Text
        ▲                                           │
        └──────── Human Runs Tools & Pastes Errors ─┘

Era 3: Agentic ML Systems (Runtime Closes the Loop)
   Task Goal ───────► ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
                      │ Runtime Loop:                        │
                      │ Context ──► Model Proposal ──► Tool  │
                      │    ▲                            │    │
                      │    └──── Sandbox Observation ───┘    │
                      └──────────────────┬───────────────────┘
                                         ▼
                                 Verified Outcome
```

### Defining the agentic system

Moving from conversational token generation to autonomous goal execution transforms the systems engineering contract between the model, the runtime, and the surrounding environment:

::: {#dfn-vol3-agentic-system .callout-definition title="Agentic system"}

***Agentic system***\index{Agentic system!definition}\index{Agentic machine learning system|see{Agentic system}} is an autonomous software system in which a runtime places a foundation model in a closed control loop with context, state, tools, and an environment—dispatching the model's authorized proposals and returning their environmental observations to subsequent calls until the task is accepted, halted, or escalated.

1.  **Significance**: The unit of systems optimization shifts from the isolated model call to the complete task trajectory. Unchecked errors compound exponentially across sequential turns (@sec-vol3-intro-horizon-arithmetic), and every attempt—whether accepted or aborted—is charged to the task's cost per accepted result.
2.  **Distinction**: In conversational interfaces, a human executes tools, verifies output, and bridges state between turns. In an agentic system, software executes these operations under delegated authority, meaning the model's output is strictly a proposal that holds zero ambient authority.
3.  **Systems pitfall**: Treating agency as a capability inherent to the model's weights. A more capable model produces more accurate candidate actions, but permission enforcement, sandbox isolation, durable state persistence, and completion verification belong entirely to the surrounding software runtime.

:::

This architectural shift forces a fundamental recalculation of core systems metrics. In classical model serving, infrastructure teams optimize for tokens per second, tail latency percentiles, and accelerator utilization. In agentic systems, the governing metrics become **task completion rate**, **cost per accepted task**, and **reliability across multi-turn horizons**. Infrastructure designed for independent requests assumes that calls incur bounded computational costs, that working state vanishes once a response returns, and that an HTTP 200 status code signals successful completion. Delegated tasks invalidate each of these assumptions: an execution spans dozens of dependent steps, accumulates gigabytes of conversational context and tool telemetry, and triggers side effects that permanently alter external systems.

## From a Useful Proposal to an Accepted Task {#sec-vol3-intro-existence-moment}

Consider a concrete engineering challenge: diagnosing and repairing an intermittent race condition in a distributed key-value store.[^fn-repair-task-benchmark] A foundation model[^fn-foundation-model-term] can inspect the issue description and propose an edit to the connection-pool locking logic. Emitting that patch text, however, leaves the repository completely untouched. Resolving the defect requires an agent to locate the relevant source files, draft an edit, execute compilers and test runners inside an isolated environment, interpret diagnostic logs when a build fails, and verify that the resulting code satisfies the repository's regression test suite.

[^fn-repair-task-benchmark]: **Repository Repair as a Benchmark Task**: SWE-bench established repository repair as a standard benchmark for agentic systems: each instance pairs a real GitHub issue with the unit and integration tests from the patch that fixed it [@jimenez2024swebench]. A candidate patch is evaluated by whether those tests pass after application. The model is never permitted to inspect the evaluation tests directly, ensuring that acceptance rests on independent, untampered evidence rather than self-reported success. \index{SWE-bench!repair task}

[^fn-foundation-model-term]: **Foundation Model**: Bommasani and colleagues introduced the term in 2021 to describe models trained on massive, diverse datasets at scale that can be adapted to an expansive range of downstream tasks [@bommasani2021opportunities]. Because a foundation model is general-purpose, its weights encode neither the security permissions nor the specific acceptance criteria of a given production task; those boundaries must be defined and enforced by the surrounding runtime. \index{Foundation model!definition}

An agentic system comes into existence precisely when software closes this interaction loop. Rather than relying on an engineer to copy prompts and error traces back and forth, the surrounding software feeds the foundation model an objective alongside fresh environmental observations, captures the model's proposed action, dispatches that action, and returns structured execution feedback to guide the next decision.

The surrounding software—the **runtime**\index{Runtime (agent)!definition}, frequently termed the agent harness—enforces the operational boundary between model reasoning and environment mutation. All execution authority resides permanently with the runtime. Because a model outputs only unstructured text or token streams, generating an operation's name confers no inherent permission to run it. The runtime parses the proposed action, verifies that it complies with current access policies, and dispatches the call through a designated tool. A **tool**\index{Tool!definition} provides a structured interface to an environmental capability, such as reading file contents, editing source code, executing a shell command, or running a test suite. @Fig-vol3-open-vs-closed-loop-control contrasts this human-mediated loop (panel A)—where an operator manually inspects outputs, runs commands, and repastes results—against the autonomous agentic architecture (panel B), where an execution runtime intercepts structured tool calls, executes them in an isolated sandbox, and feeds verified observations directly back into the context window.

::: {#fig-vol3-open-vs-closed-loop-control fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**A Person or a Runtime Closes the Loop**: In the conversational arrangement (A), the model answers and the developer runs every tool and carries each error back by hand. In the agentic arrangement (B), the runtime assembles context, receives the model's proposal, and dispatches only actions it grants; the model holds no authority, and verifier evidence returns to the runtime rather than to the model's own report." fig-alt="Two panels. Panel A, A Person Closes the Loop: a developer sends a prompt to a model endpoint and receives a patch, executes it in a local terminal, and re-pastes a compiler error to the endpoint along a dashed arrow. Panel B, A Runtime Closes the Loop: an agent runtime labeled authorizes each action sends context to a foundation model labeled holds no authority and receives a proposal, dispatches to an isolated sandbox that returns an observation, and the sandbox feeds verifiers whose evidence returns to the runtime along a dashed arrow."}
![](images/svg/open_vs_closed_loop_control.svg)
:::

Panel B represents the architectural foundation of this book. High-parameter foundation models paired with optimized inference engines provide essential proposal capabilities, but they supply only the raw computational engine. A model cannot manage its own execution authority, maintain state across tool failures, or verify the correctness of its actions against external reality. Those responsibilities fall entirely on the surrounding software architecture. Engineering an agent is therefore the discipline of designing, securing, and operating the complete closed-loop system that surrounds the model.

Analyzing and building these systems requires four foundational instruments:

1. **The Stochastic Computer**: An architectural mapping that models an agentic system after classical computer architecture, treating the foundation model as a probabilistic execution unit, the context window and external stores as a memory hierarchy, tools as input/output interfaces, and the runtime harness as the operating system kernel (@sec-vol3-intro-stochastic-computer).
2. **The H·S·A Exposure Space**: An analytical coordinate system that measures how far a delegated task departs from stateless model inference along three operational dimensions: execution horizon ($\Horizon$), persistent state ($S_0$ to $S_3$), and external authority ($A_0$ to $A_3$) (@sec-vol3-intro-hsa).
3. **The Invariant Closure Principle**: A governance rule stipulating that safety and security invariants must be mechanically enforced by the runtime below the model, while task acceptance must be verified against independent evidence above the model (@sec-vol3-intro-governance).
4. **Horizon Reliability and Cost Arithmetic**: Mathematical formulations that quantify how single-step error rates compound across multi-turn trajectories, demonstrating how retry budgets and recovery mechanisms dictate the true compute cost per accepted task (@sec-vol3-intro-horizon-arithmetic).

These four instruments operate together across production workloads. To ground their trade-offs in practice, @sec-vol3-intro-running-example traces their execution across the distributed key-value store repair alongside three diverse lighthouse applications. With those concrete profiles established, @sec-vol3-intro-book-organization introduces the structural roadmap of this book and examines the core engineering questions that govern autonomous machine learning systems.

## The Stochastic Computer {#sec-vol3-intro-stochastic-computer}

To understand how the disparate subsystems of an agentic architecture collaborate, we can look to an architecture familiar to every systems engineer: the classical computer. An autonomous task requires computational execution, working and persistent memory, interfaces to perceive and manipulate the external world, supervisory control, and mechanisms to optimize future executions from past runs. Taken together, these requirements map directly onto the classical hardware-software hierarchy.

We formalize this architectural mapping as the **stochastic computer**, diagrammed in @fig-vol3-stochastic-computer-map:[^fn-stored-program-map] the upper live execution band maps the foundation model to a CPU processor, active context and retrieval datastores to a memory hierarchy, and tool dispatch to an I/O subsystem, all mediated by an operating system runtime, while the lower across-task band structures trajectory learning and multi-agent scaling into iterative compilation passes. In this map, the foundation model acts as the central processing unit (CPU). Context engineering and external datastores represent the memory hierarchy, spanning working registers (the active context window) to secondary storage (long-term retrieval indices). Tool invocation functions as input/output (I/O) bus communication with external peripheral devices. The agent runtime serves as the operating system kernel: it schedules model calls, mediates every privileged operation, manages execution state, and enforces access control. Across tasks, trajectory learning plays the role of a profile-guided optimizing compiler, refining execution policies from traces of prior runs without modifying underlying safety boundaries. Finally, distributed agent coordination mirrors network fabrics, binding multiple autonomous agents into an integrated enterprise service.

[^fn-stored-program-map]: **The Stored-Program Organization**: Von Neumann's 1945 draft report on the EDVAC partitioned a computer into central arithmetic, central control, memory, and input/output organs [@vonneumann1945edvac]. In von Neumann's architecture, central control holds the absolute authority to fetch and execute instructions. In an agentic system, that authority is deliberately inverted: authority resides strictly within the surrounding runtime, while the learned model only proposes actions. Trust is decided outside the processor. \index{Von Neumann architecture!stochastic computer map}

::: {#fig-vol3-stochastic-computer-map fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Stochastic Computer as an Architectural Map**: The agent stack structured around traditional computing layers (marked with ≈). The live execution loop (top) executes one task trajectory turn by turn. The across-task loop (bottom) compiles evaluated trajectories into updated model policies and coordinates multi-agent scale. While the architectural analogy provides intuition, the chapters develop each subsystem through its own rigorous systems mechanisms." fig-alt="Map in two bands. The live loop band holds the model, Part I, approximately a processor; agent memory, Part II, approximately memory; the agent runtime, Part IV, approximately an operating system, spanning the band; and tool use, Part III, approximately input and output, connected to an external environment. Arrows carry proposals and context between model and runtime, stored state and records between memory and runtime, validated calls and observations between runtime and tools, and effects and results between tools and environment. Below, an across-tasks band holds learning from trajectories, Part V, approximately recompiling, fed by evaluated trajectories and sending updated weights back to the model, and agents at scale, Part VI, approximately scale-out."}
![](images/svg/stochastic_computer_architecture.svg)
:::

Crucially, the analogy breaks down at the processor—and that divergence defines the core discipline of agentic systems engineering. A conventional CPU executes instructions deterministically. Given identical registers and machine state, execution is repeatable and auditable. A foundation model, by contrast, operates stochastically by sampling tokens from an ungrounded probability distribution. Its outputs are *candidate proposals*, not certified computations. A generated response can be eloquently phrased yet factually wrong, syntactically correct yet semantically catastrophic, and nothing within the generated text itself can vouch for its own validity.

In a classical operating system, the kernel trusts the CPU to execute instructions faithfully. In an agentic system, that trust disappears: the runtime cannot trust its processor even to report its own status accurately. An ungrounded model may hallucinate a successful return code or report actions it never took. The runtime must therefore close the control loop independently: it mechanically enforces permissions below the model and verifies results against external ground truth above the model (@sec-vol3-intro-invariant-closure). Memory relationships diverge just as sharply. While a physical CPU addresses memory directly, the context presented to a model is merely a selective, lossy projection of the environment's state. Authoritative state resides in external databases, filesystems, and version-control trees; the agent's memory holds only transient working representations.

Viewing the agent as a stochastic computer clarifies where traditional systems guarantees hold and where new abstractions are required. The primary systems challenge is not simply invoking a model, but building the deterministic harness—the memory virtualization, execution sandboxes, and verification pipelines—that allows an unreliable cognitive core to drive reliable, autonomous computation.

## The H·S·A Exposure Space {#sec-vol3-intro-hsa}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_origin.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with no axis lit and the origin dot highlighted, marking a single model call."}

*Agents depart from a single model call along horizon, state, and authority.*
:::

While the architecture of a stochastic computer identifies the structural components of an agentic system, the **H·S·A exposure space** quantifies the runtime machinery that a specific workload demands. It measures how far a delegated assignment departs from an elementary, single-turn model invocation. The fundamental unit of that measurement is the primary runtime artifact of this book: the **trajectory**.

::: {#dfn-vol3-trajectory .callout-definition title="Trajectory"}

***Trajectory***\index{Trajectory!definition} is the ordered sequence of recorded states, proposed actions, runtime decisions, and observations through which one delegated task proceeds, from its initial context to its ultimate acceptance, termination, or escalation.

1.  **Significance**: The trajectory length defines the operational horizon $\Horizon$, which governs how compounding errors degrade system reliability. Furthermore, its complete span—encompassing rejected actions, retries, and failed branches—establishes the true accounting boundary when computing cost and latency per accepted task.
2.  **Distinction**: While a conversational transcript merely captures the tokens exchanged between a model and a user, a trajectory preserves the full causal history of execution. It records which action proposals the runtime approved, modified, or rejected, alongside the raw observations returned by external tools, linking every decision to the exact evidence available at that step.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Preserving only the final deliverable. Storing just the accepted patch or completed document hides the computational cost of discarded attempts, masks transient faults, and discards the intermediate verification evidence that justified accepting the work.

:::

We formalize this sequence using the compact notation

$$\ResponseThreshold = (s_0, a_0, o_1, s_1, a_1, o_2, \dots, s_H)$$

where $\StateAtTurn$ represents the recorded state available at decision step $t$, $\ActionProposal$ is the proposed action emitted by the model, and $o_{t+1}$ is the subsequent observation returned by the execution environment. Each transition from $\StateAtTurn$ to $s_{t+1}$ constitutes a single **turn**\index{Turn!definition}: one model invocation paired with the runtime's mediation of the resulting proposal. The runtime's audit log must explicitly record the disposition of every proposed action. A rejected proposal leaves external state untouched. In contrast, an action that is dispatched across a network but loses its response leaves the system in an indeterminate state, because the external tool may have committed mutations before the transport failure occurred. The notation establishes a total ordering across interactions, where each $\StateAtTurn$ reflects the runtime's partially observed view of the broader environment.

A standard model invocation is isolated: it consumes a static prompt and returns a completion. Extending that single call into an autonomous trajectory exposes the system to progressive operational risk along three physical and architectural dimensions: how long execution continues, what state persists across steps, and what external side effects the system can trigger. This book models these dimensions as the Horizon, State, and Authority (H·S·A) exposure space.

::: {#dfn-vol3-hsa-exposure-space .callout-definition title="H·S·A exposure space"}

***H·S·A exposure space***\index{HSA exposure space@H·S·A exposure space!definition} is the three-dimensional coordinate system quantifying how far a delegated task departs from an isolated model call: its horizon $\Horizon$ measured in sequential turns, the state $S_0$ through $S_3$ carried between invocations, and the authority $A_0$ through $A_3$ exercised over external systems.

1.  **Significance**: Each axis identifies a concrete operational exposure that the runtime must bound. Horizon determines how rapidly unverified errors compound, state dictates the working memory and durable artifacts carried forward, and authority establishes the maximum blast radius of an errant action. Later divisions of this book systematically address how to close these exposures: Part II governs state, Part III controls authority, and Part IV bounds horizon.
2.  **Distinction**: Coordinates in this space quantify environmental exposure rather than software architecture. System closure—the runtime validation gates, sandboxes, and compensating operations that enforce safety—represents the engineering response to these exposures rather than an independent coordinate axis.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Inferring authority from syntax or command names alone. Authority reflects the operational consequence of an action within its specific environment; an identical file deletion constitutes $A_1$ execution inside an ephemeral sandbox, but escalates to $A_3$ when executed directly against an unversioned production datastore.

:::

Horizon $\Horizon$ tracks the duration of execution in discrete sequential turns. Every additional turn provides another opportunity for invalid tool invocations, stale environment observations, and context drift; @sec-vol3-intro-horizon-arithmetic models mathematically how unchecked step-level failure rates compound into severe task-level unreliability across extended sequences. Crucially, turn count and wall-clock latency represent distinct operational budgets that require independent management. A three-turn workflow that triggers a large remote build cluster can run for hours, whereas a hundred-turn in-memory code refactoring completes in seconds. Production runtimes must meter both metrics, bounding turns to restrict error compounding and bounding wall-clock time to release compute and network resources.

State ($S_0$ to $S_3$) characterizes the data, memory, and environmental artifacts that persist across turns. At $S_0$, the system operates completely statelessly, carrying no task context past a single invocation. At $S_1$, the runtime maintains conversational working state; this includes the tokenized context window as well as inference-tier serving state, such as cached key-value (KV) attention pairs. At $S_2$, the agent manages task-local working artifacts within an isolated workspace, such as a private source tree, an ephemeral container, or an in-memory scratchpad. At $S_3$, execution interfaces with durable shared state that outlives the individual task session, such as an authoritative database, a shared object store, or a central code repository. Because realistic workloads routinely span several tiers at once, this classification establishes what data the runtime must checkpoint or isolate, determines cache invalidation boundaries, and dictates which storage system remains authoritative when local scratchpad views diverge.

Authority ($A_0$ to $A_3$) defines the blast radius of actions delegated to the task. At $A_0$, access is strictly read-only, although exfiltration remains a risk if retrieved secrets leak into output text. At $A_1$, mutations are confined entirely to a disposable workspace where unintended modifications carry zero external impact. At $A_2$, actions affect external systems, but every mutating operation is paired with an idempotent retry policy or an explicit compensating transaction[^fn-saga-compensation-intro] executed under verified preconditions. At $A_3$, the task executes non-compensable actions—such as modifying unversioned production records, issuing financial transactions, or publishing public communications—for which no automated reversal exists. Authority reflects the operational consequence within the specific execution environment rather than cosmetic command syntax. Because a trusted runtime mediates every action against an explicit per-task capability grant, restricting this grant provides the first and most cost-effective line of defense before deploying complex validation machinery.[^fn-least-privilege-mediation]

[^fn-saga-compensation-intro]: **Compensating Transactions**: Garcia-Molina and Salem introduced sagas for long-lived distributed transactions where holding locks across the entire workflow is impractical: a saga consists of a sequence of local transactions, each paired with a compensating transaction that semantically undoes earlier steps if the overall workflow aborts [@garciamolina1987sagas]. Compensation is an active forward recovery action rather than an atomic rollback; concurrent processes can observe intermediate states, and the compensating action itself may fail. An $A_2$ capability grant therefore requires an executable compensation handler before dispatching the initial mutating effect. \index{Saga!compensating transaction}

[^fn-least-privilege-mediation]: **Least Privilege and Complete Mediation**: Saltzer and Schroeder's foundational protection principles dictate that every program must operate using the smallest set of privileges necessary to complete its task (least privilege), and that every access to every object must be systematically validated (complete mediation) [@saltzer1975]. Validating capability grants on every tool invocation applies both principles to a non-deterministic model whose proposals cannot be inherently trusted. Restricting the task's initial capability grant remains the most dependable technique for minimizing potential damage when runtime verification checks fail to intercept an unsafe request. \index{Least privilege!task grant}

The coordinate space in @fig-vol3-hsa-taxonomy maps agentic workloads across three operational exposure axes: horizon ($\Horizon$, turns along the horizontal), authority ($A_0$ to $A_3$ on the vertical), and carried state ($S_0$ to $S_3$ on the depth axis). This space functions as an analytical lens rather than a rigid taxonomy: two workloads occupying the exact same cell may still demand different runtime controls if their data sensitivity, tool reliability, or catastrophic failure thresholds diverge. Furthermore, altering the execution environment can shift a task into a completely different cell even when its foundation model and turn horizon remain identical, as demonstrated in example \ref{exmp-01-hsa-incident}. The four reference workloads plotted across the space represent the lighthouse applications developed throughout this book and introduced in @sec-vol3-intro-lighthouses.

::: {#fig-vol3-hsa-taxonomy fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The H·S·A Exposure Space**: Horizon ($\Horizon$, turns), carried state ($S_0$ to $S_3$), and authority ($A_0$ to $A_3$) map the operational departures of an agent from an isolated model call. Plotted positions and closure mechanisms represent illustrative task configurations rather than intrinsic properties of each workload class. The formal task contract and failure consequences dictate necessary runtime controls. System closure represents the engineering response to these exposures rather than an independent coordinate axis." fig-alt="Three-axis diagram with authority on the vertical axis from A0 read access to A3 irreversible external action, horizon in turns on the horizontal axis from H equals 1 to H at least 1,000, and state on a diagonal depth axis from S0 stateless to S3 durable shared state. Four workload cards are placed in the space, showing the support, remediation, repair, and research agents."}
![](images/svg/hsa_taxonomy.svg)
:::

::: {#exmp-01-hsa-incident .callout-example title="A working copy and the only copy"}

**Scenario**: A coding assistant must repair a software defect while preserving adjacent, uncommitted edits authored by a developer. Consider two execution environments: an isolated, ephemeral sandbox containing a working copy of the project vs. direct access to the developer's sole authoritative workspace. The foundation model, repair objective, and expected turn horizon remain identical in both configurations. In each case, the assistant issues a command to delete files while cleaning up intermediate build artifacts.

**Diagnosis**: Inside the ephemeral sandbox, the source files constitute $S_2$ working state and the mutation authority is bounded at $A_1$. Tearing down the sandbox discards any erroneous modifications without corrupting the developer's original files. In the authoritative workspace, however, that identical command targets $S_3$ state. If the deleted files contain unique, unstaged edits missing from version control history, the operation immediately escalates to $A_3$ irreversible data destruction. Version control alone does not prevent this loss, as uncommitted working-tree changes lack snapshots. A resilient systems contract grants the agent access strictly to an isolated clone, excludes unrelated edits from the agent's context, and reserves the integration of reviewed patches for a separate gate. The runtime must enforce that isolation boundary through tool authorization rather than relying on prompt instructions asking the model to exercise caution.

**Systems lesson**: The failure boundary shifted fundamentally even though the model, prompt, and turn horizon remained unchanged. Automated test suites evaluate functional behavior, and diff reviews verify patch cleanliness, but neither technique prevents an unauthorized deletion command from obliterating working state. Sound systems engineering enforces safety at the infrastructure boundary—preventing destructive operations from reaching authoritative state—rather than relying on post-hoc verification to detect irreversible side effects.

:::
## Invariant Closure {#sec-vol3-intro-governance}

A foundation model operating within an agentic loop generates fluent, plausible proposals, but it cannot certify their safety or correctness. This fundamental limitation creates the central governance challenge of agentic architecture: **invariant closure**. When the model cannot validate its own outputs, the surrounding system must guarantee operational integrity. Invariant closure resolves this division of responsibility through a two-sided architecture: safety constraints are mechanically enforced below the model, while task completion is verified against independent evidence above the model.

### The fail-plausible fault {#sec-vol3-intro-fail-plausible}

Invariant closure primarily defends against the **fail-plausible fault**\index{Fail-plausible fault!definition}: the output appears well formed and credible while the intended property remains unsatisfied.[^fn-unsignaled-failure-taxonomy] Consider an autonomous repository repair loop: an agent terminates its execution with a confident, well-reasoned summary declaring that a race condition is fixed, even though the underlying defect persists. The generated patch might be syntactically immaculate yet eliminate thread safety by deleting a critical synchronization lock. Alternatively, a test suite might exit with return code zero only because the model commented out failing assertions. In both cases, the system encounters a fault that appears completely credible to superficial inspection.

Classical fault models highlight why this failure pattern demands a distinct systems category. In distributed systems, a *fail-stop* component halts when it faults, enabling a supervisor to detect the failure through missing heartbeats or nonzero exit codes [@schlichting1983failstop]. A *Byzantine* component may exhibit arbitrary or deceptive behavior, but classical fault tolerance counteracts this through redundant voting across independent replicas [@lamport1982byzantine].[^fn-failstop-byzantine-faults] A fail-plausible fault evades both defenses. Because the model process neither crashes nor halts, fail-stop monitors register success. Furthermore, sampling repeatedly from the same foundation model does not produce independent Byzantine replicas: models trained on similar data share systematic blind spots, generating correlated failure modes. The fail-plausible fault is thus an unsignaled semantic failure tailored to look like success.

[^fn-failstop-byzantine-faults]: **Fail-Stop and Byzantine Faults**: Schlichting and Schneider defined a fail-stop processor as one that halts on failure without first making an erroneous state transition, so that other processors can detect the halt [@schlichting1983failstop]. Lamport, Shostak, and Pease showed that reaching agreement when some components may send arbitrary, conflicting messages requires more than two-thirds of the components to be correct, the origin of the $3f+1$ replica bound for tolerating $f$ such faults [@lamport1982byzantine]. \index{Fault model!fail-stop}\index{Fault model!Byzantine}

[^fn-unsignaled-failure-taxonomy]: **Signaled and Unsignaled Failures**: The standard dependability taxonomy classifies failures by detectability as well as by kind: a signaled failure raises a warning when the service goes wrong, and an unsignaled one does not [@avizienis2004basic]. A fail-plausible fault is an unsignaled content failure (the delivered result is wrong and nothing announces it), so a runtime that watches only for crashes, timeouts, and error codes will record it as a success. \index{Fault model!unsignaled failure}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/fault_models_margin.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Three stacked cards. Fail-stop: halts, and missing progress reveals it. Byzantine: arbitrary, and independent replicas outvote it. Fail-plausible, highlighted in red: looks like success and needs an outside check."}

*Each fault model is caught by a different defense; only an independent check catches a plausible wrong answer.*
:::

To prevent fail-plausible faults from corrupting system state, the execution environment enforces **zero ambient authority**\index{Zero ambient authority!definition}: the model holds no standing privileges of its own, and every external side effect must pass through an explicit grant checked by the runtime.[^fn-confused-deputy-authority] Generated tokens cannot authorize commands, alter the runtime's execution records, or declare acceptance. Instead, the runtime gathers environmental evidence strictly through designated tools and deterministic checks. For repository repair, this requires separating raw patch text from the applied file diff, as well as isolating model-authored summaries of test execution from actual process exit codes.

[^fn-confused-deputy-authority]: **The Confused Deputy**: Hardy described a compiler that held a license to write files in its own directory; a user passed it the name of the billing file as an output path, and the compiler, acting with its own authority rather than the user's, overwrote the billing records [@hardy1988confused]. Authority that comes from where a program runs rather than from the request it serves can be steered by whoever supplies the names, which is exactly the position of a model whose tool calls run with host credentials while it reads untrusted text. \index{Confused deputy!ambient authority}

Every external check establishes a bounded claim that is narrower than the overarching task objective. A clean compilation step demonstrates only that the program conforms to grammar and type rules under a specific build configuration. A passing regression test records only that the implementation executed successfully for the specific inputs and thread schedules tested. As Dijkstra observed, testing can reveal the presence of defects, but never prove their absence\index{Verification!testing vs. proof} [@dijkstra1970structured].

### The invariant closure principle {#sec-vol3-intro-invariant-closure}

The working-copy comparison in example \ref{exmp-01-hsa-incident} separates preventing an unauthorized action from deciding whether an outcome meets engineering requirements. A filesystem boundary mechanically prevents writes outside the assigned workspace. Whether a patch inside that workspace repairs a race condition is a distinct assertion requiring empirical evidence of program behavior. **Invariant closure**\index{Invariant closure!definition}\index{Principle!invariant closure} assigns both responsibilities to explicit mechanisms around the model rather than relying on model self-assurance.

::: {#pri-invariant-closure .callout-principle title="Invariant closure"}

**Invariant**: Constraints never rest on the model; bounds close mechanically below it, acceptance on evidence above it. Each enforced bound names the property and assumptions under which it holds, and each acceptance decision names the evidence standard it applies. Without either, a trajectory of $\Horizon$ steps, each correct with probability $1-\SmallConstant$, succeeds only with probability
$$ \Pr(\text{success}) = (1-\SmallConstant)^{\Horizon} $$
while a bound or a check turns a violating step into a rejected attempt instead.

**Implication**: Unchecked reliability decays exponentially with horizon, an attrition that model scaling alone cannot overcome. The runtime mediates permitted effects and resource use independently of the model's compliance. It accepts completion only when evidence meets the task contract, preserving the distinction between a passing check and a guarantee beyond that check's coverage. The contract itself is adopted by authorized people: the model can draft it but cannot adopt, relax, or certify against it. Greater operational exposure requires stronger justification for both the boundaries and the evidence.

:::

Mechanical enforcement establishes concrete execution boundaries. A filesystem restriction prevents writes to protected paths, provided all file operations pass through the enforcement layer and its isolation assumptions hold. This mechanism governs where modifications land, but leaves the correctness of those modifications as a separate question. Similarly, schema validation confirms that a tool request is syntactically well formed, while authorization remains an independent check. The systems design rule is to keep each enforced property narrower than the complete task claim and explicitly name the guarantee it provides.

Acceptance decisions rely on evidence organized across distinct **closure evidence levels**\index{Closure evidence levels!definition}. At the base level, an agent's self-report represents an unverified claim rather than an empirical observation of the environment. The classical end-to-end argument governs this distinction [@saltzer1984endtoend]: an end-to-end task property can be validated only by an endpoint equipped with complete task requirements. Correct behavior at a lower layer—such as generating well-typed code—cannot certify end-to-end correctness. Static analysis checks structural and type invariants without executing the code. **Visible tests**\index{Visible test!definition} execute cases that the agent can inspect directly; while valuable for iterative diagnosis, they expose test cases that candidate solutions can overfit against. In contrast, **sealed tests**\index{Sealed test!definition} withhold test definitions and run within tamper-proof sandboxes, preserving evaluation integrity. Formal verification establishes that an implementation satisfies an explicit mathematical model, though confirming that the specification reflects true user intent remains an external human judgment. These levels define the grounding of a claim rather than a rigid hierarchy: an exhaustive sealed test suite provides more practical confidence than a mathematical proof derived from an incomplete specification.

In the race-condition repair, passing a sequential unit test yields evidence only for single-threaded execution. Sealing that test protects the assertions from modification, but does not broaden its coverage. Establishing that the concurrency defect is resolved requires running multi-threaded stress workloads that force thread interleavings under varied execution schedules. Human code review then examines operational assumptions that the test harness cannot probe. Because an automated verdict can be fully repeatable yet structurally incomplete, acceptance claims must remain strictly bounded by what the test infrastructure measured.

Certain completion criteria cannot be reduced to executable boolean predicates and require qualitative evaluation. An automated or human evaluator scores these outcomes against an explicit rubric, documenting decision ownership and epistemic uncertainty while mechanical permission bounds remain in force. When candidate evidence falls short of the task contract, the runtime reports an unresolved outcome or escalates to human operators; it never treats a plausible narrative as a substitute for verified completion. Different validation mechanisms exhibit markedly different reliability profiles. Moreover, intermediate verification checks placed within a multi-turn trajectory reset the error compounding analyzed in @sec-vol3-intro-horizon-arithmetic, making rigorous invariant closure indispensable as task horizons grow.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Measuring a grader's false-acceptance rate against independent reference assessment is developed in @sec-vol3-evaluation-grading-errors.
:::

### The five-part task specification contract {#sec-vol3-intro-five-part-contract}

A simple instruction such as "repair the race condition" leaves critical engineering boundaries undefined. A proposed patch might remove thread synchronization entirely, passing a sequential regression check while exacerbating concurrency failures under production load. Similarly, an agent issued a cleanup directive might purge scratch files in a disposable sandbox, or inadvertently delete uncommitted source files in a shared repository. An unadorned goal cannot distinguish constructive solutions from catastrophic side effects. Before an execution engine dispatches any autonomous action, the system requires an explicit specification defining what resources may be mutated and what evidence is required to accept the final output.[^fn-wiener-machine-purpose]

[^fn-wiener-machine-purpose]: **Wiener's Warning on Delegated Purpose**: In 1960 Wiener argued that when a mechanical agency acts too fast and irrevocably for anyone to intervene before the action completes, "we had better be quite sure that the purpose put into the machine is the purpose which we really desire" [@wiener1960]. The warning binds hardest where authority is irreversible, which is why the contract that follows is written and adopted before the loop runs rather than repaired after an effect lands. \index{Wiener, Norbert!delegated purpose}

A task specification transforms underspecified intent into an enforceable systems contract. We formulate this as a five-part tuple, $\TaskContract = \langle \LongmessageGapPerByte, \Environment, \PermittedActions, \AvailableObservations, \CompletionCriteria \rangle$, which cleanly separates the desired objective from the execution environment, delegated permissions, permitted observations, and acceptance criteria. This structural separation is necessary because natural language instructions communicate intent without providing the runtime mechanisms required to authorize execution or verify task fulfillment.[^fn-design-by-contract]

[^fn-design-by-contract]: **Design by Contract**: Meyer framed a software component's interface as a contract of preconditions the caller must establish, postconditions the supplier guarantees, and invariants both preserve, each written as a checkable assertion [@meyer1992applying]. The task contract borrows the structure but not the trust: in classical design by contract the supplier's own code checks its postconditions, whereas here the supplier is the model, so the completion criteria must be checked by the runtime and tools rather than asserted by the component that produced the result. \index{Design by contract!task contract lineage}

::: {#dfn-vol3-task-contract .callout-definition title="Task contract"}

***Task contract***\index{Task contract!definition} is the explicit specification of a delegated task that separates its goal, environment, permitted actions, available observations, and completion criteria, so that the runtime, not the model, decides what may execute and when the task is done.

1.  **Significance**: The completion criteria define what counts as accepted, which fixes the denominator of cost per accepted task. Two systems, or two versions of one system, can be compared only under the same contract.
2.  **Distinction**: A prompt communicates intent to the model; a contract is enforced by the runtime and the tool environment. The same sentence can appear in both, but only the contract constrains what executes.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Writing the permitted actions into the prompt alone. The model reads the limit, and the host process still allows everything its credentials allow.

:::

In the repository repair task, the goal $\LongmessageGapPerByte$ includes an explicit **negative scope**\index{Negative scope!definition}—the set of existing system behaviors and invariants that must remain undisturbed outside the reported defect. The environment $\Environment$ identifies the source baseline, runtime dependencies, and the designated workspace where edits occur. Permitted actions $\PermittedActions$ authorize bounded file edits, directory inspection, and test runner invocations, while denying network egress and write access to parent directories. Available observations $\AvailableObservations$ restrict returned payloads to source excerpts, bounded test logs, and Git diffs. Finally, completion criteria $\CompletionCriteria$ define the sealed test suites that must pass alongside human review gates for unmeasured behaviors. @Tbl-contract-template grounds these five components in concrete systems artifacts.

| Contract Component         |      Formal Symbol       | Systems Role                                        | Concrete Engineering Artifact                    |
|:---------------------------|:------------------------:|:----------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|
| **Goal**                   |           $\LongmessageGapPerByte$            | Desired end state and explicit negative scope       | Repair request that preserves unrelated behavior |
| **Environment**            |      $\Environment$      | Target state and execution conditions               | Source baseline and designated working copy      |
| **Permitted Actions**      |   $\PermittedActions$    | Operations and resources within delegated authority | Allowed edit paths and test commands             |
| **Available Observations** | $\AvailableObservations$ | Information the task may obtain and return          | Source excerpts, bounded test output, and diff   |
| **Completion Criteria**    |  $\CompletionCriteria$   | Evidence and decision rule for accepting the result | Required regression checks and review decision   |
: **Five-Part Task Specification Contract**: Each component answers a distinct systems question for the repair task, cleanly decoupling intent, execution context, authority, visibility, and verification. {#tbl-contract-template tbl-colwidths="[20,18,30,32]"}

Each component of the contract prevents a specific systems failure mode. Omitting a negative scope from the goal invites degenerative solutions, such as silencing a concurrency bug by removing the failing assertion or deleting multi-threaded access paths altogether. Lacking an isolated environment specification, agent edits and ad hoc dependency installations pollute shared host state, destroying experimental reproducibility. Without explicit action boundaries, tool dispatch defaults to the ambient authority of the host process. Unbounded observations permit sprawling search outputs that flood the model's context window, degrading reasoning performance and evicting critical instructions. Finally, omitting formal completion criteria forces the runtime to rely on the model's self-reported success as its termination signal.

Dynamic environments with non-stationary state are manageable when the contract explicitly distinguishes observable task state from exogenous background events, as in live service incident triage. Observation constraints must also differentiate empty query results from truncated responses. If the runtime truncates a voluminous test log to fit token budgets, it must inject explicit truncation metadata into the prompt; otherwise, the model may treat the omission of an error message as proof that no error occurred.

Operational resource bounds and termination rules necessarily accompany the contract. Every delegated task requires turn budgets, wall-clock execution deadlines, monetary token spend limits, and deterministic error-handling policies for resource exhaustion. Halting on an exhausted resource budget produces an unresolved outcome rather than a failure or silent termination: the runtime preserves the intermediate diff, logs the incomplete verification checks, and escalates to human engineers for intervention.

Drafting a contract also exposes the boundaries of what can be safely delegated. Subjective directives such as "improve maintainability" cannot be evaluated by automated predicates alone. In such cases, the system architect must establish measurable proxy metrics, assign a qualified human reviewer, or exclude the subjective decision from autonomous execution entirely. The primary function of the task contract is to make these operational boundaries explicit so that the runtime can enforce them deterministically.

Subsequent chapters implement each facet of this architecture. In @sec-vol3-tool-calling, we formalize permitted actions and structured observation schemas. In @sec-vol3-sandboxes, we design isolated container and virtual machine environments to safely execute untrusted side effects. In @sec-vol3-agent-harness, we construct orchestration harnesses that enforce task goals, operational budgets, and stopping rules. Finally, @sec-vol3-evaluation establishes the statistical and empirical evidence pipelines required by formal completion criteria.

The invariant closure principle and the five-part task contract establish the governance framework required for autonomous execution. Mechanically enforcing isolation below the foundation model protects shared infrastructure, while verifying empirical evidence above the model guarantees deliverable quality. Yet rigorous governance introduces concrete systems overhead: running sealed regression suites, provisioning ephemeral execution sandboxes, and verifying intermediate invariants consume runtime latency and compute budgets. Evaluating these engineering trade-offs requires analyzing the quantitative dynamics of multi-turn execution, where horizon compounding and verification economics determine the ultimate cost per accepted task.

## Reliability and Cost over a Horizon {#sec-vol3-intro-horizon-arithmetic}

A realistic agentic trajectory spans dozens of sequential turns, with each turn building directly on observations and state modifications from the preceding step. A misdiagnosed deadlock trace leads the model to inspect the wrong source file; an erroneous patch to that file cascades into compilation failures or silently corrupts unrelated business logic. Because foundation models generate fluent rationalizations even when mistaken, nothing in the model's generated text signals the exact moment execution derailed. An extended autonomous task can easily fail even when individual per-turn accuracy appears exceptionally high.

Elementary probability demonstrates how rapidly unchecked errors compound, explaining why the invariant closure principle requires intermediate verifiers inside the execution loop. Suppose each of $\Horizon$ sequential steps is correct with probability $1-\SmallConstant$, errors are statistically independent, and no step is verified before subsequent steps build upon it. The overall task succeeds only if every intermediate step succeeds:

$$\Pr(\text{success}) = (1-\SmallConstant)^{\Horizon}$$ {#eq-vol3-horizon-compounding}

@Eq-vol3-horizon-compounding applies classic series-reliability analysis[^fn-unreliable-components-reliability] to the sequential turns of a trajectory. We call the resulting reliability collapse **horizon compounding**\index{Horizon compounding!definition}. Statistical independence is an idealization; in practice, errors correlate and models occasionally recover from bad states. Yet even when correlation alters the exact numerical path, the governing dynamic endures: unchecked execution decays exponentially with horizon length (notebook \ref{nbk-01-horizon-compounding}).

[^fn-unreliable-components-reliability]: **Reliable Systems from Unreliable Components**: Von Neumann posed the problem in 1956 for logic networks whose every element errs with some fixed probability, so that errors accumulate through the depth of the computation [@vonneumann1956probabilistic]. His remedy interleaved redundant computation with "restoring organs" that re-establish a correct signal at intervals, keeping the error bounded however deep the network grows. Checks inside a trajectory play the same structural role: each one stops error accumulation so that overall reliability depends on the distance between checks rather than on the total horizon length. \index{Reliability!unreliable components}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/horizon_compounding_margin.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Curve of unchecked task success against horizon in turns at the notebook step accuracy, falling from about nine in ten tasks at the short horizon to about one in three at the long horizon, with both points labeled."}

*At a fixed step accuracy, unchecked success falls exponentially with the horizon.*
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-intro-horizon-compounding
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HORIZON COMPOUNDING FOR UNCHECKED STEPS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @eq-vol3-horizon-compounding and @nbk-01-horizon-compounding.
# │ Goal: Show task success falling with horizon at a fixed step accuracy.
# │ Show: Success at two horizons; step error and eps*H needed for a target.
# │ How:  (1 - eps)^H with independent, unchecked steps; ~exp(-eps*H).
# │ Note: Hypothetical step accuracy, not a measured model property.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_math, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent

class HorizonCompounding:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario inputs) ────────────────────────────────────────
    step_ok = 0.99  # hypothetical per-step probability of a correct step
    h_short, h_long = 10, 100  # horizons in turns
    target = 0.90  # task success rate to hold at the long horizon

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    eps = 1 - step_ok
    p_short = step_ok**h_short
    p_long = step_ok**h_long
    eps_needed = 1 - target ** (1 / h_long)
    eps_ratio = eps / eps_needed
    eps_h_needed = eps_needed * h_long  # the product that sets reliability

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(p_long < 0.5 < target <= p_short, "Long horizon must fail most tasks; short must meet target")
    check(eps_needed < eps and eps_ratio > 5, "Holding the target must need a much lower step error")
    check(abs(eps_h_needed + math.log(target)) < 0.01, "eps*H must match -ln(target) in the small-eps limit")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    step_ok_str = fmt_percent(step_ok, style="prose")
    eps_str = fmt_percent(eps, style="prose")
    h_short_str, h_long_str = fmt_int(h_short), fmt_int(h_long)
    target_str = fmt_percent(target, style="prose")
    p_short_str = fmt_percent(p_short, precision=1, style="prose")
    p_long_str = fmt_percent(p_long, precision=1, style="prose")
    eps_needed_str = fmt_percent(eps_needed, precision=2, style="prose")
    eps_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(eps_ratio, precision=1)
    p_short_math = fmt_math(rf"{fmt(step_ok, precision=2)}^{{{h_short}}} \approx {fmt(p_short, precision=3)}")
    p_long_math = fmt_math(rf"{fmt(step_ok, precision=2)}^{{{h_long}}} \approx {fmt(p_long, precision=3)}")
    eps_needed_math = fmt_math(rf"\epsilon = 1 - {fmt(target, precision=2)}^{{1/{h_long}}} \approx {fmt(eps_needed, precision=5)}")
    eps_h_math = fmt_math(rf"\epsilon H \approx {fmt(eps_h_needed, precision=3)}")
```

::: {#nbk-01-horizon-compounding .callout-notebook title="Horizon compounding"}

**Problem**: Each step of a repair agent is correct with probability `{python} HorizonCompounding.step_ok_str`, independently, and no step is checked before the next one builds on it. What fraction of tasks succeed at horizons of `{python} HorizonCompounding.h_short_str` and `{python} HorizonCompounding.h_long_str` turns, and what per-step error rate would hold the longer horizon at `{python} HorizonCompounding.target_str` success?

**Math**: By @eq-vol3-horizon-compounding, `{python} HorizonCompounding.p_short_math`, so `{python} HorizonCompounding.p_short_str` of tasks succeed at `{python} HorizonCompounding.h_short_str` turns, while `{python} HorizonCompounding.p_long_math` leaves `{python} HorizonCompounding.p_long_str` at `{python} HorizonCompounding.h_long_str` turns. Holding `{python} HorizonCompounding.target_str` at `{python} HorizonCompounding.h_long_str` turns requires `{python} HorizonCompounding.eps_needed_math`, about `{python} HorizonCompounding.eps_needed_str` per step and `{python} HorizonCompounding.eps_ratio_mult_str` lower than the assumed `{python} HorizonCompounding.eps_str`. For small $\SmallConstant$, $(1-\SmallConstant)^\Horizon \approx e^{-\SmallConstant \Horizon}$, and the requirement reads `{python} HorizonCompounding.eps_h_math` at any horizon.

**Systems insight**: The product $\SmallConstant \Horizon$, not step accuracy alone, sets task reliability. A tenfold longer horizon demands a tenfold lower per-step error to hold the same success rate. The cheaper engineering knob is usually the unchecked horizon itself: an intermediate check that rejects a bad step and retries it resets the compounding window. Consequently, an extended task fortified with reliable checkpoints behaves like a sequence of short, independent segments rather than one vulnerable chain. Supplying and enforcing those checks is the primary responsibility of the runtime, as formalized by the invariant closure principle (\ref{pri-invariant-closure}).

:::

Checking converts a silent failure into an explicit, rejected attempt—and a rejected attempt still consumes real resources. Suppose each attempt at a task is accepted with probability $\AcceptanceProbability$, independently of earlier attempts, and the runtime retries until one is accepted. The number of attempts follows a geometric distribution with mean $1/\AcceptanceProbability$. Each attempt costs $\AttemptCost$ in expectation, tallying model tokens, tool execution, test sandboxes, and human review—all of which a failed attempt consumes just as completely as a successful one. The expected **cost per accepted task**\index{Cost per accepted task!definition} is therefore

$$\CostPerAcceptedTaskEff = \frac{\mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]}{\AcceptanceProbability}$$ {#eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task}

In production systems, runtimes enforce bounded retry budgets, meaning unrecoverable tasks eventually terminate without acceptance. The cohort ratio introduced in @sec-vol3-intro-fallacies computes this effective cost directly from empirical spend and acceptance tallies. Even in its basic form, @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task highlights an essential systems trade-off between unit model pricing and task-level verification (notebook \ref{nbk-01-cost-per-accepted}).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Whole-trajectory cost and the cohort cost per accepted task, which charges failed and abandoned attempts to the accepted ones, are developed in @sec-vol3-agent-economics-accounting.
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-intro-cost-per-accepted
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COST PER ACCEPTED TASK: TOKEN PRICE VS. ACCEPTANCE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task, @nbk-01-cost-per-accepted,
# │          @chk-vol3-intro-governance, and the accounting pitfall.
# │ Goal: Compare halving token prices with raising acceptance probability.
# │ Show: Baseline, both interventions, the break-even acceptance, and the
# │       understatement from charging only the accepted attempt.
# │ How:  C_eff = E[C_attempt] / p_acc with retry until acceptance.
# │ Note: Hypothetical prices and probabilities, not a provider schedule.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_math, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_pp, fmt_usd

class CostPerAccepted:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario inputs) ────────────────────────────────────────
    c_model = 1.30  # scenario USD of model tokens per attempt
    c_other = 0.80  # scenario USD per attempt for sandbox, tests, and review
    p_acc = 0.40  # probability an attempt is accepted
    token_cut = 0.5  # fraction of token price removed by a cheaper tariff
    p_acc_better = 0.60  # acceptance after a context or tool improvement
    other_cut = 0.5  # checkpoint: fraction of sandbox/test/review cost removed
    p_acc_step = 0.10  # checkpoint: acceptance gain from a tool change

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    c_attempt = c_model + c_other
    token_share = c_model / c_attempt
    attempts = 1 / p_acc
    c_eff = c_attempt / p_acc
    c_attempt_cheap = c_model * (1 - token_cut) + c_other
    c_eff_cheap = c_attempt_cheap / p_acc
    c_eff_better = c_attempt / p_acc_better
    p_breakeven = p_acc / (1 - token_cut * token_share)
    gain_pp = round((p_breakeven - p_acc) * 100)  # whole points, for prose
    understate = c_eff / c_attempt  # accepted-attempt-only accounting error
    c_eff_ck_other = (c_model + c_other * (1 - other_cut)) / p_acc
    c_eff_ck_acc = c_attempt / (p_acc + p_acc_step)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(c_eff_better < c_eff_cheap < c_eff, "Raising acceptance must beat the token cut here")
    check(p_acc < p_breakeven < p_acc_better, "Break-even acceptance must lie between the two rates")
    check(abs(p_breakeven - c_attempt / c_eff_cheap) < 1e-9, "Break-even forms must agree")
    check(abs(c_eff_ck_other - c_eff_ck_acc) / c_eff < 0.05, "Checkpoint options must be a close call")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    c_model_str = fmt_usd(c_model, precision=2)
    c_other_str = fmt_usd(c_other, precision=2)
    c_attempt_str = fmt_usd(c_attempt, precision=2)
    c_attempt_cheap_str = fmt_usd(c_attempt_cheap, precision=2)
    p_acc_str = fmt_percent(p_acc, style="prose")
    p_acc_better_str = fmt_percent(p_acc_better, style="prose")
    p_breakeven_str = fmt_percent(round(p_breakeven, 2), style="prose")
    token_share_str = fmt_percent(round(token_share, 2), style="prose")
    gain_pp_str = fmt_pp(gain_pp, precision=0)
    p_acc_step_pp_str = fmt_pp(p_acc_step * 100, precision=0)
    attempts_str = fmt(attempts, precision=1)
    c_eff_str = fmt_usd(c_eff, precision=2)
    understate_mult_str = fmt_multiple(understate, precision=1)
    c_eff_math = fmt_math(rf"{fmt(c_attempt, precision=2)} / {fmt(p_acc, precision=2)} = {fmt(c_eff, precision=2)}")
    c_eff_cheap_math = fmt_math(rf"{fmt(c_attempt_cheap, precision=2)} / {fmt(p_acc, precision=2)} \approx {fmt(c_eff_cheap, precision=2)}")
    c_eff_better_math = fmt_math(rf"{fmt(c_attempt, precision=2)} / {fmt(p_acc_better, precision=2)} = {fmt(c_eff_better, precision=2)}")
    p_breakeven_math = fmt_math(
        rf"{fmt(p_acc, precision=2)} / (1 - {fmt(token_cut, precision=1)} \times {fmt(token_share, precision=2)}) \approx {fmt(p_breakeven, precision=2)}"
    )
```

::: {#nbk-01-cost-per-accepted .callout-notebook title="Cheaper tokens or more acceptances"}

**Problem**: An attempt at the repair task spends `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_model_str` on model tokens and `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_other_str` on the sandbox, tests, and review, and is accepted with probability `{python} CostPerAccepted.p_acc_str`. Which lowers cost per accepted task more: halving the token price, or raising acceptance to `{python} CostPerAccepted.p_acc_better_str` through a context or tool improvement?

**Math**: The baseline attempt costs `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_attempt_str`, and the task needs `{python} CostPerAccepted.attempts_str` attempts on average, so @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task gives `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_eff_math` dollars per accepted task. Halving the token price lowers the attempt to `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_attempt_cheap_str`, giving `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_eff_cheap_math` dollars. Raising acceptance at the original attempt cost gives `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_eff_better_math` dollars. Tokens are `{python} CostPerAccepted.token_share_str` of the attempt, so the price cut matches an acceptance of `{python} CostPerAccepted.p_breakeven_math`.

**Systems insight**: Cost per accepted task is inversely proportional to acceptance probability, but scales only linearly with component prices. Halving the token price removes half of the tokens' `{python} CostPerAccepted.token_share_str` share, producing an improvement equivalent to gaining just `{python} CostPerAccepted.gain_pp_str` of acceptance (`{python} CostPerAccepted.p_acc_str` to `{python} CostPerAccepted.p_breakeven_str`). Any context enhancement or tool refinement that lifts acceptance beyond that threshold outperforms the price cut, because higher acceptance amortizes sandbox overhead, environment setup, and verification spend across fewer discarded runs. Systems engineers must evaluate interventions by their net effect on $\CostPerAcceptedTaskEff$ under a rigorous acceptance contract, never by inference tariffs alone.

:::

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/cost_per_accepted_margin.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Three horizontal bars of cost per accepted task from the notebook: the baseline is longest, halving the token price shortens it, and raising acceptance shortens it slightly more."}

*Acceptance divides every cost in an attempt, so a modest gain in it can outweigh halving the token price.*
:::

@Eq-vol3-horizon-compounding and @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task form the quantitative bedrock for systems design throughout this book. @Eq-vol3-horizon-compounding governs how rapidly reliability deteriorates across unchecked trajectories, while @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task establishes the economic threshold for architectural mechanisms. An intermediate check, a sandbox boundary, or a prompt cache justifies its system overhead when it lowers $\mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]$ by a larger ratio than it degrades $\AcceptanceProbability$, or conversely, when it increases $\AcceptanceProbability$ by a factor that outstrips its added per-attempt cost.

Neither equation depends on how control decisions are generated. Both apply equally to deterministic programs with hardcoded control flow and to autonomous loops where foundation models choose each subsequent action. That structural neutrality makes them the decisive instrument for choosing between static workflows and dynamic agentic loops.

### Workflows vs. model-directed loops {#sec-vol3-intro-workflow-vs-loop}

The software repair task illustrates both predictable mechanics and dynamic exploration. Initializing a working copy, fetching dependencies, and executing static analysis can follow a **fixed workflow**\index{Fixed workflow!definition}, where the sequence of operations is specified in advance. In contrast, diagnosing an intermittent race condition requires inspecting arbitrary source files, formulating test hypotheses, and evaluating runtime logs based on observations that unfold dynamically. A **model-directed loop**\index{Model-directed loop!definition}, in which the model chooses its next tool invocation based on intermediate trajectory observations, becomes valuable precisely at these divergent branches—provided its empirical acceptance gains exceed the variance and token overhead it introduces.

A fixed workflow is not limited to static linear scripts: it can evaluate conditional branches, manage retries, and dispatch parallel tasks, provided its control graph is defined in advance. Because the model calls embedded within a workflow remain stochastic, a deterministic control graph guarantees neither reproducible outputs nor bounded wall-clock latencies. When comparing a fixed workflow against a model-directed loop, systems architects must evaluate both under identical task contracts and acceptance verifiers. By @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task, a model-directed loop is justified only when its open-ended exploration raises $\AcceptanceProbability$ by a greater proportion than its additional model calls inflate $\mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]$.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Economic feasibility envelopes for choosing between deterministic workflows and model-directed loops are developed in @sec-vol3-selection-economics.
:::

Authorization policies must be decoupled from the control architecture that selects the steps. A fixed workflow can require human authorization before executing an external side effect, just as an autonomous diagnostic loop can operate entirely unprompted within an isolated sandbox. The runtime permits exploratory actions within a constrained boundary while gatekeeping irreversible operations such as production deployment. An approved execution grant merely authorizes an action to run; it does not validate the correctness of the resulting state, which still requires independent post-condition verification.

::: {#chk-vol3-intro-governance .callout-checkpoint title="Changing the task boundary"}

A repair agent can inspect and edit a disposable working copy and return a patch for review. Its contract grants no access to the deployment service.

**Reading the boundary**

- [ ] **Authority**: The task now includes deployment. Which authority level does it move to, and which permission decision must be added that no passing test can supply?
- [ ] **State**: The workspace turns out to hold the only copy of unrelated edits. Which exposure changes, and which single change to the grant removes it?
- [ ] **Acceptance evidence**: A sealed sequential test passes after the race-condition repair. Which claim does it support, and what further evidence would you require before accepting?
- [ ] **Control policy**: Which steps of the repair would you assign to a fixed workflow, and which decision must stay model-directed?

**Pricing the choice**

- [ ] **Cost per accepted task estimate**: An attempt costs `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_attempt_str`, of which `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_other_str` is sandbox, tests, and review, and `{python} CostPerAccepted.p_acc_str` of attempts are accepted. Estimate the cost per accepted task if you halve that `{python} CostPerAccepted.c_other_str`, and again if a tool change raises acceptance by `{python} CostPerAccepted.p_acc_step_pp_str`. Which would you fund?

:::

Treating agent reliability and execution cost as coupled functions of trajectory length and acceptance probability establishes a rigorous baseline for system design. These quantitative trade-offs explain why real-world agent architectures depend less on unconstrained model autonomy than on bounded execution graphs, robust intermediate verifiers, and disciplined resource accounting across realistic workloads.

## The Running Example and Four Lighthouses {#sec-vol3-intro-running-example}

To ground the architectural instruments without introducing disjointed scenarios in every chapter, this book organizes its systems analysis around four recurring workloads. The automated repository repair introduced in @sec-vol3-intro-existence-moment serves as the primary running example. Following this repair task across its execution turns shows how core runtime mechanisms operate on concrete problems. Three additional workloads then map out operational regimes that repository repair alone cannot exercise.

### The trajectory as the systems management boundary {#sec-vol3-intro-trajectory-systems-boundary}

Tracing the repair task across turns exposes how proposals, side effects, and observations interact over time. Execution begins when the runtime provisions an isolated working copy of the repository and supplies the initial task description. The model proposes running the failing test. After validating that this command is authorized, the runtime invokes the test runner and records its output. When the runner reports a deadlock, the runtime supplies the diagnostic output to the next model call. The model then proposes inspecting the connection-pool implementation, and the returned source code reveals the locking logic that requires repair.

Guided by this inspection, the model proposes a patch. Before modifying the working copy, the runtime verifies that the edit targets permitted files. This step underscores a foundational separation of concerns: the model's generated diff is merely a proposal, the modified file is an effect, and the tool's execution report is an observation. When a subsequent compilation attempt reports an unclosed bracket, that observation directly steers the next decision. The model proposes a corrected patch, which the runtime applies before rerunning the build. Once compilation succeeds and visible unit tests pass, the runtime collects regression evidence using an immutable test suite that the editing tools cannot touch. It then records the resulting deliverable alongside these verification records. If the results satisfy the contract's acceptance criteria, the runtime submits the repair; otherwise, it can continue iterating, abort, or escalate to a human engineer.
